articles.title: AI Is Coming for You, But You Can Fight Back: The Hidden Costs of Artificial Intelligence
articles.author: Frieda Afary
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Artificial intelligence is being sold to the public as the next great technological revolution, promising unprecedented productivity, scientific breakthroughs, and solutions to some of humanity's most difficult problems. But who benefits from this transformation, who pays its costs, and who gets to decide how the technology is deployed? Those questions drove a panel titled “AI Is Coming for You, But You Can Fight Back” at the fourth annual Left Coast Forum, held October 2–4, 2026, at California State University, Los Angeles. Moderated by Iranian American writer, librarian, and socialist feminist Frieda Afary, the discussion featured environmental scientist Pablo Ortiz Partida of the Union of Concerned Scientists, education researcher Nick Rabb, and environmental journalist Bill Kelly. Together, they challenged the narrative that artificial intelligence represents inevitable progress, arguing instead that its rapid expansion reflects decisions made by powerful corporations and institutions, often without meaningful public participation. AI Is Coming For You (1:08:07) The Environmental Costs Hidden Behind the Cloud Pablo Ortiz Partida began by dismantling one of the technology industry's central illusions: that the digital world exists somewhere apart from the physical environment. The cloud, he explained, consists of enormous buildings filled with computers requiring electricity, cooling systems, water, and extensive infrastructure. The new generation of hyperscale data centers being constructed for artificial intelligence represents something fundamentally different from conventional computing facilities. Some proposed complexes encompass hundreds or thousands of acres and require electricity comparable to that consumed by substantial population centers. Ortiz Partida described how these facilities can strain water supplies, increase electricity demand, produce air pollution through diesel backup generators, and subject neighboring communities to constant industrial noise. He also discussed the trade-offs involved in cooling systems. Technologies that reduce electricity consumption may require more water, while those conserving water may consume additional energy. Crucially, he emphasized that most of a data center's water footprint can occur indirectly through electricity generation rather than at the facility itself. That means regulations addressing only water consumed on-site may overlook much of the environmental burden. The consequences are not distributed equally. Communities living near data centers may experience rising energy costs, noise, pollution, and additional heat while receiving relatively few of the promised economic benefits. Ortiz Partida distinguished between targeted applications of machine learning that can assist climate research and medicine and the far more resource-intensive generative AI systems driving much of today's infrastructure expansion. His argument was not that every application of artificial intelligence is harmful, but that society must evaluate its benefits against its environmental and social costs. Related: AI, Surveillance and War: Who Is Emerging Technology Really Serving? Is AI Undermining Education and Critical Thinking? Nick Rabb, a postdoctoral researcher studying AI and education, offered an equally troubling assessment of the technology's impact on classrooms. Rabb examined the California State University system's multimillion-dollar agreement with OpenAI to provide ChatGPT access across its campuses. The arrangement was promoted as a way to provide personalized tutoring, improve educational opportunities, and help instructors manage their workloads. But Rabb questioned whether the evidence justified those promises. After reviewing research on large language models in educational settings, he concluded that their use frequently undermines learning, especially when students depend on them to perform intellectual tasks they need to master themselves. Students who already possess strong study habits and critical-thinking abilities may benefit in limited circumstances, he explained. Those who lack such foundations may become increasingly dependent on technology that performs their thinking for them. Rather than closing educational inequalities, widespread AI adoption could therefore deepen them. Rabb also warned that language models reproduce biases embedded in their training material and can reinforce users' existing assumptions. Students must learn to evaluate evidence, recognize flawed arguments, and challenge ideological assumptions—not simply accept plausible-sounding answers generated by commercial systems. His criticism extended beyond classroom performance to the governance of public universities. Rabb described how faculty committees and task forces had examined the implications of AI, yet major institutional decisions could still be imposed from above. For him, this illustrated a broader democratic problem: corporations and university administrators increasingly determine how education is organized, while educators and students have limited power over those decisions. AI's Expanding Ecological Footprint Environmental journalist Bill Kelly widened the discussion beyond data centers to the global supply chains required to build them. Kelly, author of Smogtown: The Lung-Burning History of Los Angeles and The People's Republic of Chemicals , argued that the environmental costs of artificial intelligence begin long before a server is switched on. The metals needed for computer equipment are extracted from mines, frequently in countries in the Global South where environmental protections and labor standards may be weak. Mining can destroy landscapes, contaminate water supplies, and expose nearby communities to hazardous pollution. Those materials must then be transported, refined, manufactured into components, and shipped again before reaching data centers. Each stage requires energy and generates additional environmental damage. Kelly also emphasized the short useful lives of advanced computing equipment. Servers containing substantial quantities of valuable metals may be replaced after only a few years, contributing to an already enormous global electronic-waste problem. He warned that the coming expansion of robotics could multiply these pressures. For Kelly, the underlying issue is an economic system dependent on continuous growth, even as humanity approaches or exceeds critical ecological limits. He urged governments to distinguish socially beneficial uses of AI from applications designed primarily to maximize profits, eliminate jobs, expand surveillance, or intensify consumption. Related: AI "Friends" Are a Big Joke—But You Shouldn't Laugh Workers, Surveillance, and the Question of Power The discussion repeatedly returned to the consequences of artificial intelligence for working people. Kelly pointed to warehouse surveillance systems capable of monitoring employees' movements and hospital staffing technologies that can prioritize cost reduction over patient care. He also raised concerns about artificial intelligence replacing performers and other entertainment workers, potentially depriving them of employment and benefits. The panel connected these developments to the expansion of surveillance technologies and the growing power of corporations to control workplaces, public institutions, and information. In the audience discussion, participants drew comparisons with the nineteenth-century Luddites, whose resistance to industrial machinery was rooted in conflicts over labor, ownership, and economic power. The question was not simply whether new machines could perform human tasks, but whether technological development would enhance human freedom or strengthen existing systems of exploitation. Fighting Back Means Reclaiming Democratic Control Despite their criticisms, the panelists did not suggest that resistance was futile. Rabb described students who deliberately avoid using language models because they recognize the importance of developing their own intellectual abilities. Participants emphasized the need for technological, environmental, and economic literacy—particularly the ability to distinguish genuine scientific advances from exaggerated corporate promises. Kelly called for enforceable environmental standards, responsible supply chains, longer equipment lifespans, and restrictions on socially destructive applications of artificial intelligence. The larger challenge, however, was political. The panel suggested that decisions about technologies affecting education, employment, public health, civil liberties, and the environment cannot remain exclusively in the hands of corporate executives and institutional administrators. The question is not whether artificial intelligence will continue developing. It is whether democratic societies can assert control over how that development proceeds, whose interests it serves, and what costs humanity is willing to bear. At the Left Coast Forum, the message was that fighting back begins by rejecting technological inevitability and insisting that people—not corporations or algorithms—determine the future.

articles.title: U.S. Complicity Shaped a Catastrophe
articles.author: Rick Chertoff, Dick Price, Robert Corsini
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Israeli assault on Gaza cannot be understood by beginning the story on October 7, 2023. That was one of the central arguments advanced during a panel titled “The Gaza Genocide” at the fourth annual Left Coast Forum, held October 2–4, 2026, at California State University, Los Angeles. Featuring longtime Jewish peace activist Rick Chertoff and historian Dr. Mahmood Ibrahim, the discussion challenged familiar narratives about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and examined the history of dispossession, occupation, failed diplomatic initiatives, and American military support that preceded the current catastrophe. The panel also confronted a question that has become increasingly urgent: What will it take to end the destruction of Gaza and establish a future in which Palestinians and Israelis can live with equal rights and security? The Gaza Genocide (23:10) The Conflict Did Not Begin With Hamas One of the panel's central arguments was that Israel's conflict with Palestinians long predates the establishment of Hamas in 1987. “There was no Hamas in 1948,” one panelist emphasized, referring to the year Israel was established and hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were displaced during what Palestinians call the Nakba, or catastrophe. Nor did Hamas exist during the 1967 war, when Israel occupied the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, and East Jerusalem. This history, the speakers argued, undermines explanations that present Hamas as the fundamental cause of Palestinian suffering. Ibrahim traced the organization's emergence to political developments during the 1980s, including the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood, the first Palestinian intifada, and widespread frustration with the inability of secular Palestinian organizations to achieve liberation. He challenged the simplified claim that Israel created Hamas. Instead, he argued, Israeli authorities recognized opportunities to exploit divisions between religious and secular Palestinian movements, weakening the possibility of a unified Palestinian political response. Those divisions would eventually become central to the breakdown of efforts to achieve Palestinian self-determination. Related: The Erasure of Palestine Gaza and the Failure of the Peace Process The panel examined Israel's 2005 withdrawal of approximately 8,000 settlers from Gaza and the subsequent deterioration of conditions in the territory. Although the withdrawal removed Israeli settlements from Gaza, it did not establish Palestinian sovereignty. Israel retained extensive control over Gaza's borders, airspace, and maritime access, while Egypt also controlled access through its border. After Hamas won the 2006 Palestinian legislative elections and subsequently consolidated control over Gaza, Israel intensified restrictions on the territory. The panelists described the repeated Israeli military assaults that followed as part of a continuing strategy of containment and destruction rather than a genuine effort to resolve the underlying conflict. They referred to the Israeli military expression “mowing the lawn,” used by some Israeli security strategists to describe recurring operations intended to degrade Palestinian armed groups' capabilities. For the speakers, that expression illustrated the normalization of periodic military violence against an already confined population. They also recalled the Great March of Return demonstrations in 2018 and 2019, when Palestinians gathered near Gaza's perimeter fence demanding the right of return and an end to the blockade. Israeli forces killed more than 200 Palestinians and injured thousands during those protests, according to United Nations reporting. The panelists argued that these events, together with expanding Israeli settlement activity, violence in the West Bank, and diplomatic initiatives that marginalized Palestinian demands, formed an essential backdrop to October 7. Understanding that history, they maintained, is necessary without excusing attacks on civilians. Related: J.D.’s Rant to Israel: “Wake Up and Smell the Reality!” The American Role: Weapons, Money, and Political Protection A particularly forceful exchange emerged when an audience member challenged the effectiveness of continued discussion while Palestinians were being killed. The participant demanded that the United States stop supplying Israel with weapons and financial assistance, insisting that verbal condemnations were insufficient. The speakers largely agreed with the urgency of that demand. Chertoff emphasized that political change rarely happens immediately. Drawing on his experience with social movements, he compared the struggle to end American support for Israel's military operations with the long campaign against the Vietnam War. Mass movements, he argued, often require years of organizing before they can force political leaders to change course. Yet he also suggested that public opposition to American policy toward Israel has developed far more rapidly than opposition to the Vietnam War did. The discussion highlighted campaigns to block weapons shipments, pressure Congress, support the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, and elect candidates willing to challenge unconditional military assistance to Israel. The speakers also criticized the role of political messaging in maintaining support for the assault on Gaza, arguing that misleading and inflammatory claims have helped justify continued military operations. For the panelists, exposing those narratives is inseparable from the work of building an effective movement for Palestinian rights. Is a Two-State Solution Still Possible? The discussion concluded with a question about the political future of Israel and Palestine. Asked whether he supported a two-state solution, Chertoff answered unequivocally that he did not. His objection was not simply ideological. He argued that the fragmented territories envisioned for a Palestinian state would lack the geographical continuity, economic independence, and freedom of movement necessary for meaningful sovereignty. He described the Palestinian state imagined under the Oslo framework as effectively a “telephone booth with a flag.” A territory whose borders, trade, transportation, and access to the outside world can be controlled by another government, he suggested, cannot function as a genuinely independent nation. But Chertoff did not offer a rigid alternative blueprint. Instead, he argued that Palestinians and Israelis must ultimately determine their own political arrangements, whether through a single democratic state, a confederation, or another structure. What matters, he maintained, is ending coercive domination and creating conditions in which people can negotiate their future as equals. The panel also acknowledged the challenge posed by divisions within Palestinian political leadership and the absence of a unified strategy for liberation. Yet the speakers suggested that demanding a comprehensive political program from a population experiencing massive destruction overlooks the conditions under which Palestinians are struggling to survive. Related: The Mamdani Win and the Losing Ethos of the Democratic Party From Outrage to Organized Political Power The discussion's most important conclusion was that the future of Gaza cannot be separated from American political choices. The United States is not merely an outside observer. Through military assistance, diplomatic protection, and its influence over regional politics, Washington possesses enormous power to shape events. The panelists argued that Americans who oppose the destruction of Gaza must therefore move beyond expressions of outrage toward sustained political organization capable of changing U.S. policy. The struggle, as they described it, is not simply about securing a ceasefire or negotiating another temporary arrangement. It is about confronting the structures of military domination, dispossession, and unequal rights that have defined Palestinian life for generations. The question left hanging over the room was whether Americans can build a movement strong enough to force their government to stop enabling those structures. For Chertoff and Ibrahim, the answer depends less on another round of diplomatic promises than on the willingness of ordinary people to organize, exert pressure, and demand a fundamentally different relationship between the United States, Israel, and Palestine.

articles.title: Workers Can Govern, but They Need Power First
articles.author: Jared Abbott
articles.content: According to data from a sweeping new study of working-class legislators by political scientists Nicholas Carnes and Noam Lupu, only about 2 percent of legislators across the world’s democracies held a working-class job — which the authors define as manual, service, or clerical work — before getting into politics. Yet as the authors document in their new book , Keeping Workers Off the Ballot: How Democracy Undermines Working-Class Representation , about seven in ten jobs in a typical democracy are working-class jobs, from construction workers and truck drivers to servers, cashiers, receptionists, data-entry clerks, day laborers, and street vendors. In the United States, working-class people make up more than half of the labor force but just 5 percent of candidates for state, county, and local office. In Brazil, workers represent more than 70 percent of the labor force but just 8 percent of candidates for the national legislature. Drawing on a wide range of previous scholarship and original analysis, Carnes and Lupu show why having more workers in office matters. Politicians who have had working-class jobs back more pro-worker economic legislation, cabinets with more working-class ministers build more generous welfare states, and citizens trust legislatures less when they include fewer workers. In short, “when workers don’t hold office, economic policies and outcomes are better for the haves and worse for the have-nots.” Keeping Workers Off the Ballot focuses on the obvious follow-up question: If working-class officeholders are so good for working people, why are there so few of them? Their answer is pretty demoralizing. The problem, they argue, contrary to the dominant view of many on the Left, isn’t money, the weakness of unions, particular electoral rules, or an aversion to working-class candidates among voters. Instead, the reason lies deeper, embedded in the logic of electoral democracy itself: running for office is personally grueling, demanding time, money, and a willingness to put one’s job and income at risk that people in working-class jobs can rarely afford, and party gatekeepers rationally pass over those least likely to weather the storm of an electoral campaign. Together these two processes ensure that working-class candidates will always face major headwinds that limit their success. The book’s major contribution is showing how hard it is to elect legislatures that represent working people. But its central claim is more fatalistic than its own evidence supports, and its remedies leave out a key path that has historically given working people real political leverage: working-class organization. Where Is the Leak in the Candidate Pipeline? Carnes and Lupu begin by dispensing with a range of other explanations for low working-class representation, starting with the idea that workers simply don’t have what it takes to govern. The authors reject this and other “deficit explanations” by showing that workers are nearly as likely as others to have the traits of successful candidates, that they are just as interested in running, and that they are no less popular with voters. They are equally skeptical of country-level explanations. Using an original database of legislators in ninety-seven democracies in 2016–18, the scholars conclude that variation in types of electoral systems and the strength of left parties make no significant difference in the prevalence of working-class legislators. By contrast, they find that public financing of elections and union density do matter, but the authors judge their effects too small to make a meaningful difference. The real problem, according to Carnes and Lupu, comes before the ballot box: “The vast majority of the screening out [of working-class candidates] seems to happen at the point when people get on the ballot.” They offer two primary reasons. The first is what the authors call the hidden costs of campaigns. Running for office means giving up time, privacy, income, and certainty about the future, not to mention risking embarrassment and reputational damage. These costs weigh most on workers: in the authors’ surveys in Mexico and Canada, 29 percent of high-potential working-class respondents said they would worry about giving up their job or income to run, compared with 14 percent of equally qualified professionals. The second factor holding back workers from running for office is the strategic logic of party gatekeeping. With limited resources, parties go after “low-hanging fruit”: people they already know and trust, who seem likely to make good politicians and to have a comparatively easy time running a campaign. Under pressure to win now, even sympathetic party leaders pass over candidates who can be less easily presented as sure bets, and those are disproportionately working class. In surveys across ten democracies in the Americas, Carnes and Lupu found that the most promising working-class respondents were far less likely than comparable professionals to have been encouraged to run by political elites: 12 percent versus 34 percent. These forces are so powerful, Carnes and Lupu argue, that “even if workers run and win and hold office successfully,” elections “will always exert a gravitational pull” against them. Stronger unions, public financing of elections, and lower inequality, they argue, “will only matter on the margin.” Electing many workers requires “extraordinary and unusual alignments of political forces.” Unions to the Rescue? What are those alignments? Above all, they consist of durable partnerships in which parties build formal channels for recruiting candidates straight out of strong, centralized labor unions. These unions give working-class candidates the money and backing to shoulder the burdens of running, and equally important, they seek out worker-candidates and sell them to other party insiders, in effect bypassing the usual logic of gatekeeping. Britain’s Labour Party is a case in point. By 1929, more than a quarter of the House of Commons had previously held working-class jobs. British unions sponsored worker candidates, turned out voters for them, paid for their campaigns, hired local party staff to work for them, and sometimes topped up their salaries, while local Labour parties chose from a union-drawn list of candidates who came with union money. Germany’s Social Democratic Party (SPD) worked much the same way, reserving safe list positions for union officials. In 1969, about 16 percent of the Bundestag came from working-class jobs. If these parties could effectively get workers elected in partnership with the labor movement, why can’t parties do the same today? Carnes and Lupu’s answer is that such arrangements are historically rare and effectively irreproducible. In both Britain and Germany, white-collar unions eventually displaced industrial ones, professionals replaced manual workers on party benches, and leaders like Tony Blair and Gerhard Schröder cut unions’ role in choosing parliamentary candidates. As a result, today even the strongest unions only manage to get modest numbers of their members into office. Law of Democracy or Product of Neoliberalism? Carnes and Lupu make a strong case that the ceiling for working-class representation in contemporary democratic politics is low, but are their sobering conclusions about the meager possibilities of building real working-class power through national legislatures justified? Let’s start with the mechanisms Carnes and Lupu identify as the key barriers to greater working-class representation. By their own estimates, moving from no public financing to the most generous system observed would raise workers’ share of a national legislature from near zero to about 5 percent, and high unionization would raise it to about 9 percent. Similarly, their estimate for the impact of inequality, which imagines a country where the bottom half of earners takes home half of all income (much higher than a typical democracy today), yields about 7 percent. Parties matter, too: 10 percent of legislators from parties whose supporters are mostly working class have held manual, hospitality, or other working-class jobs. And parties that champion workers and unions the most in their party platforms have legislative delegations that are about 15 percent working class, according to Carnes and Lupu. Against a global average of 2 percent, these are not small differences. In addition, the authors test each of these factors individually and set them aside because none has a big enough impact in isolation. They do raise the possibility that “some combination of country-level traits could together explain” worker underrepresentation but don’t pursue this possibility. Yet their own history of the British Labour Party shows how country-level factors can work together to produce strong worker representation in office: a mass union movement funded and sponsored worker candidates, local parties chose candidates from union-generated lists, and the party depended on working-class votes for success. None of these alone would have led to workers occupying a quarter of parliamentary seats. Nor is it clear why a union-party partnership is the only combination of factors that could lead to a higher share of workers in office, given that Carnes and Lupu’s data show public financing, lower inequality, and parties’ dependence on working-class voters also matter. Many of the strategies the authors recommend have also never been tried at scale. By their own account, there are few if any political scholarships or seed-money programs aimed at working-class candidates in the United States, and only a handful of union-run candidate schools exist across the country. Even short of anything approaching class parity, gains of the magnitude that are likely achievable through these mechanisms would substantially improve the quality of working-class representation. Working-class candidates who got on the ballot wouldn’t just be those able to run the gauntlet that liberal democracies put before them. Timing matters, too. The book’s cross-national data is a 2016–18 snapshot in time, taken when unions were weak, inequality was high, and left parties had long since weakened their ties to labor. Britain and Germany elected more workers when unions were both large and powerful inside parties. By contrast, union membership today is far lower, and where it remains comparatively high, unions have largely lost their influence over the nominating process. The modest union effect the authors find may thus say more about the particular period they study than about what strong, politically embedded unions can do to boost working-class representation. The authors’ case study of Britain also suggests these gains are stickier than their “boom-and-bust” account implies. The number of working-class MPs did collapse when Labour lost four-fifths of its seats in the early 1930s, but the authors’ own figure shows their share climbed back to above a quarter of the Commons by 1945, was around 15 to 20 percent through the 1970s, and remained above 10 percent until the 1990s. Half a century of meaningful working-class representation is hardly a blip. The effect of gatekeeping is similarly contingent. The authors offer powerful evidence that recruiters favor professionals, but that is not, in itself, evidence that the “fundamental logic” of elections works against workers. In an era of extreme class segregation and professionalized politics, party officials mostly know professionals. When unions are central to a party’s coalition, gatekeepers’ networks fill with working-class people, and when candidate schools train union members, the pool of “low-hanging fruit” begins to include more workers: the New Jersey AFL-CIO program counts nearly 1,400 election victories since 1997. And with trust in government near record lows , candidates with a working-class background can be an asset that even the most cynical operatives may find appealing, which is one of the reasons we’re seeing more high-profile working-class candidates in the 2026 electoral cycle. Class Quotas and Citizens’ Assemblies to the Rescue? The book’s final chapter turns to solutions. The authors examine steps unions and parties could take: pipeline programs like New Jersey’s, “political scholarships” to replace lost wages, seed money for working-class candidates, a right to return to one’s job after campaigning, and worker committees inside parties. But they see these as “temporary solutions,” since elections will keep working against workers once reformers’ efforts begin to stall. Ultimately, Carnes and Lupu turn to two structural fixes that, they argue, would remove the obstacles keeping workers out of legislatures: worker quotas and citizens’ assemblies. With a quota, the authors note, if a party must nominate a worker for a seat, “it doesn’t really matter whether workers have a harder time running.” Likewise, citizens’ assemblies chosen by lot skip campaigns altogether and can ensure roughly equal participation across class. The trouble is that quotas are unlikely to be easier to win than the alternatives the authors consider inherently limited. They acknowledge that quotas require “the hard work of constructing political coalitions to pass laws and amend constitutions.” But a coalition strong enough to make legislators, most of them professionals, hand seats to workers would also be strong enough to strengthen workers’ right to organize and so substantially grow the labor movement, or to pass a wave of pro-worker legislation. Mandatory quotas are thus not a shortcut around building working-class power, but rather contingent upon it. And without that power, quotas may guarantee workers seats but not influence, since party leaders could simply fill seats with working-class candidates prepared to advance their agenda rather than pro-worker politics. Citizens’ assemblies raise a different problem. They are very good at producing bodies that look like the public: Austria’s 2022 Citizens’ Climate Assembly was about as likely to include college graduates as the public at large. But the authors never say how much power assemblies would hold. They describe sortition as a way to “select leaders without holding elections,” yet the assemblies they point to make recommendations that elected officials can take or leave. Ireland’s assembly paved the way for the 2018 referendum that repealed the country’s abortion ban, but only because politicians chose to put the question to voters. An assembly with real authority would have to be won from those same politicians, which brings us back to building working-class power. Assemblies can be useful on the margins, but no amount of deliberation by randomly chosen citizens will change the balance of political power unless workers have real leverage behind them. At worst, these reforms could help legitimize parties that ignore workers’ interests by letting them appear to give workers a stronger voice. Strikingly, for a book whose central historical finding is that workers are more likely to reach office when strong unions put them there, Keeping Workers Off the Ballot never recommends building stronger unions. There is nothing on labor law, organizing, or how working-class movements might regain the political leverage they once had. Nevertheless, Carnes and Lupu have written an indispensable book on a question the Left cannot afford to ignore. They are right that working-class representation does not happen by accident, that it is not mainly about workers’ talents or voters’ prejudices, and that it depends on institutions that put workers’ interests at the center of candidate recruitment. But the absence of workers from office is not a gravitational constant. It is a measure of the weakness of the labor movement and of parties’ choice to abandon it. Workers will hold power in national legislatures again when they first regain power outside of them. Ultimately, the point of electing more workers is not to help parties win the next election, but rather to give working people a direct role in how their lives, communities, and country are governed. And that depends on building power in workplaces and communities, not just winning elections. articles.title: What Happens to Art
articles.author: William J. Astore
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. There’s a kerfuffle about art being political, with journalists and writers I respect, such as Matt Taibbi and Caitlin Johnstone , coming down on opposite sides of the issue. Johnstone puts it bluntly : “I have no respect for this idea that art is somehow separable from politics. ALL art is political when you live in a genocidal dystopia, because all your expression exists in relation to our freakish civilization.” While I sympathize with Johnston’s opposition to the ongoing genocide in Gaza, and have written plenty of articles myself against this genocide, I don’t define all my writing as reducible to politics. Writing is a form of self-expression, a creative act, and though we are all influenced by the society in which we live, that doesn’t mean that everything we write (or otherwise create) is necessarily a political expression. Of course, art can have political meaning, often by design, occasionally not. But if all art is political, doesn’t that suggest that art is simply politics by another name? Related: AI, Surveillance and War: Who Is Emerging Technology Really Serving? Without looking at dictionary definitions, I think of art as a creative act. An act of imagination, an expression of the human spirit. We draw, we write, we sculpt, we make music, we dance, etc., as forms of expression. The richness of that expression--those creative acts--shouldn’t be reduced to political expressions. The best art transcends politics. It’s like saying all sports is politics. Sure, sports can have political meaning, but sport is something more than political expression. For example, there is a physical joy to sports, as a form of expression, that denies its reduction to politics. This idea that everything is politics or political is a dangerous one. It seems to be driven by those who want to attack others for the “wrong” politics in their art. Defining art as politics seems a handy formula for the dictator to outlaw or repress art that is considered dangerously “political” or otherwise threatening to political power. Related: America’s New Space Race Is About Weapons, Not Exploration Recall that in the 1930s Adolf Hitler attacked “Jewish” art as degenerate. Included in that was jazz as well, treated by the Nazis as a degenerate form of music, associated as it was with Black and Jewish musicians. Art, put simply, is something more than politics, and those who create art shouldn’t be defined or judged or constrained or condemned by the politics of critics who see everything through a political lens. Bracing Views

articles.title: Colombia’s President Wants US Boots on the Ground
articles.author: Carlos Cruz Mosquera
articles.content: In the ten weeks since multimillionaire lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella was inaugurated as Colombia’s president, the country has undergone a significant political shift with respect to asserting its national sovereignty, with Colombia returning to — and potentially deepening — its subordinate position vis-à-vis the United States. Less than a week after the change of government in Colombia, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced a major shift in US-Colombian military cooperation, stating at a press conference that de la Espriella had approved an agreement for joint operations in Colombia. US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) commander General Francis Donovan had met with Colombia’s highest-ranking military officials by the end of the month to begin planning those joint operations against armed groups. There have since been reports — some confirmed directly by the Colombian government and US Southern Command — of US military personnel and aircraft operating in Colombia. The prospect of a renewed US military presence has provoked alarm among significant sections of Colombian society, particularly on the Left, which has a long tradition of opposition to US interventionism in the region. De la Espriella’s policy has therefore faced growing scrutiny and opposition. Opposition leader Iván Cepeda has submitted a formal complaint to the Colombian courts, arguing that the president’s actions concerning the joint military operations have violated the political rights of Colombians. Return of the Iron Fist US military presence has been justified primarily through the language of defense and security, one that obscures underlying strategic interests . Colombia is not only a key regional ally but an important source of natural resources, including oil and coal. US imperialism in Colombia was challenged, albeit unevenly, by Gustavo Petro’s progressive administration, particularly in its approach to US military involvement and the resolution of Colombia’s armed conflict. Through what it termed Total Peace, Petro’s government sought to move away from the US-backed militarist approach toward negotiated solutions with the country’s various armed groups. However, these efforts faced significant limitations, both due to the progressive government’s shortcomings in implementing its peace agenda as well as the pressure exerted by powerful factions of Colombia’s traditional ruling class. The resulting setbacks helped pave the way for this renewed militarist offensive, bringing Colombia closer to the very approach that has historically underpinned US involvement in the country. The significance of the latest developments is not simply that Colombia is returning to closer military cooperation with the United States. After all, Bogotá has maintained close military ties with Washington since the mid-twentieth century. What is different, and particularly significant from the perspective of Colombian sovereignty, is the apparent willingness of the new government to permit direct US military operations on its territory. More importantly, lacking coalitional power and the clientelist networks of traditional parties, de la Espriella has not sought approval from the Senate for such operations — approval that, according to the Colombian Constitution, is required for even the transit of foreign troops in the country. What Makes This Different From Past US Interventions? Colombia has long been one of the United States’ closest military partners in Latin America. For decades, Washington has provided the country with more US Department of Defense training and equipment than any other country in the region while embedding US advisers within its military and security institutions. This relationship dates back at least to 1949, when the United States established formal army and air force missions in Colombia. The relationship, however, has not always been limited to training and advice. From the 1950s, US military assistance became common to Colombia’s counterinsurgency campaigns. Although Washington and Bogotá have maintained that the historical US military assistance to Colombia is about regional security and the fight against criminal groups, it has always been deeply linked to the persecution of left-wing political leaders and movements. One of the first joint operations was the infamous 1955 military offensive against insurgent peasants in Villarrica, in which the Colombian Air Force used US-supplied aircraft in bombing operations. The United States also supplied several military advisers to the operation, which was high in casualties and displaced at least one hundred thousand peasants. The extent of US involvement subsequently deepened. Signed in 2000, Plan Colombia expanded Washington’s military assistance to the Andean country on an unprecedented scale. Its official emphasis was counter-narcotics, although US assistance also became deeply intertwined with Colombia’s counterinsurgency campaign against guerrilla organizations. US support included military equipment, training, intelligence, and institutional assistance. At the same time, however, US law explicitly prohibited military personnel and civilian contractors from participating directly in combat operations. That distinction became increasingly blurred in practice. From the late 1990s, US intelligence and targeting capabilities were deeply integrated into Colombian military operations, including from US special operations personnel. Nevertheless, at least formally, the model remained one in which Colombian forces conducted the combat operations and the United States provided intelligence and logistical support. What is novel about the developments since August 7 is the erosion of this historical distinction. The question is not whether the United States has intervened militarily in Colombia prior to today; that much is clear. What we seem to be moving toward is even more direct involvement: US forces operating alongside local troops in operations on Colombian soil. US Troops on the Ground There is at least one instance in which the presence of US military aircraft and troops have been confirmed without the constitutional approval of the Senate. In late August, three US Marine Corps Venom helicopters and US troops entered Colombian airspace, specifically deployed to the port city of Tumaco on the Pacific Coast. The US Southern Command itself published pictures of the incursion, calling it an “operational site survey” and part of a broader deployment “by US military forces within their area of responsibility, in support of the Western Hemisphere Joint Task Force.” According to US officials, they are operating in the country to combat the narcotics trade and armed groups considered a threat to the United States and its allies. As part of the mission, General Donovan, commander of the US Southern Command, met with Colombia’s highest-ranking officers. According to reports from Colombia, the aircraft and their military personnel transported Donovan to his meetings in Colombia and then also transported the general and his Colombian counterparts to a meeting in Ecuador and back. That is to say, the incursion by the US military into Colombian territory was with the evident consent and authorization of the Colombian government. Colombia’s Minister of Defense, Jorge Eduardo Mora, who met with Donovan during the visit, subsequently stated that the “visit reaffirms the commitment to continue working together against narcoterrorists, the cartels, and all criminal organizations that seek to sow violence.” Studies have found that militarized counter-narcotics policies in Colombia often fail to achieve lasting reductions in coca cultivation while displacing production into new areas, exacerbating armed conflicts and endangering rural and Afro-Colombian communities. But the strategic significance of the US military presence on Colombia’s southern Pacific coast extends beyond counter-narcotics. Tumaco is a commercial port and the Pacific terminal of the Trans-Andean oil pipeline, linking Colombia to Ecuador’s oil infrastructure. Its role in energy and commodity trade, alongside growing US involvement in Colombian-Ecuadorian security cooperation, highlights the region’s broader economic and geopolitical importance. Another important report, details of which are yet to be confirmed, is of an operation that took place in Catatumbo, northeastern Colombia, on September 15. The Colombian Armed Forces undertook a mission to rescue eight hostages held by the Ejército de Liberación Nacional (ELN) one of the major guerrilla groups that remain in operation in the country. De la Espriella and the army’s official announcement failed to mention US involvement, but Colonel Fabio Ojeda, director of one of the Colombian units involved, subsequently stated that SOUTHCOM had participated in the operation. Reports suggest that US involvement entailed the use of drones, though the details remain unclear. Considering the announcements and the fast pace with which the US military is becoming more deeply enmeshed in Colombia, government officials appear to be heading toward an agreement like that seen in Ecuador under far-right Washington ally Daniel Noboa, in power since 2023. As reported recently, US military presence in Ecuador now involves on-the-ground heavily armed US personnel taking part in counter-narcotics operations. What About Congress? In Ecuador, President Noboa’s administration has found a more straightforward loophole with which to bypass the constitutional restrictions on foreign military presence. Ecuador’s government argues that the operations US Army personnel have taken part in are temporary and therefore do not breach constitutional restrictions, which focus on more permanent installations or the use of the country’s military bases. Colombia’s Constitution, Article 173(4), is somewhat more precise, specifying that Senate approval must be sought for foreign troops to transit within its borders. As well as more generally denouncing the announcement made by Hegseth on the new military cooperation agreement, Colombia’s opposition leaders have reacted with dismay at the unauthorized presence of US military aircraft and troops. Opposition leader Iván Cepeda, who lost the presidential election to de la Espriella by two hundred thousand votes, announced a constitutional protection action ( tutela ) against the government over the presence of the US military in Tumaco. Cepeda’s legal action against the de la Espriella government is only the latest and most prominent in a line of similar formal actions taken by the opposition, particularly representatives of his Pacto Histórico party. Walter Aguirre and Congressman Erick Velasco have both submitted similar legal actions. Moreover, Velasco recently took the government to court after the Defense and Foreign Affairs offices failed to respond to an information request concerning the matter. On September 21, the judge ruled in favor of Velasco and ordered Defense Minister Jorge Mora to respond within forty-eight hours. Mora and the government have yet to respond to the request. Plan Colombia 2.0? When Plan Colombia was first implemented, Colombia’s left-wing opposition had nothing like the representation it has in Congress today. The Pacto Histórico, despite losing the presidential election to de la Espriella, remains the largest political force in the country’s legislature. Without the political dominance that the Right enjoyed during the years of Plan Colombia, de la Espriella’s government is now confronting a legislature in which its opponents have both the numbers and the constitutional mechanisms to challenge executive power. This is what makes the current dispute over US military involvement so consequential. The legal challenges brought by Cepeda, Velasco, and others may appear limited in the face of an administration determined to press ahead with its security agenda. But they are testing something larger than the legality of any single operation. They are testing whether Colombia’s constitutional institutions can impose meaningful limits on the executive when foreign military power is involved. Importantly, it is the wider public — grassroots movements, anti-imperialist groups, and the millions who voted for the Pacto Histórico — that empowers political representatives like Cepeda to oppose this form of foreign interference. De la Espriella’s administration will therefore face opposition not only from representatives in Congress and the Senate but also from a broader popular movement with a long history of mobilizing against threats to Colombian sovereignty. In anticipation of popular mobilizations against these and other policies pursued through undemocratic means, the government has approved a decree granting police additional powers to restrict “violent protests.” The term is defined so broadly that it includes “disruptions to critical infrastructure,” leaving considerable scope for the repression of dissent. The opposition’s legal challenges will help determine what Colombia’s constitutional restrictions on foreign military intervention actually mean in practice, and whether the country’s institutional checks on executive power can hold under a government willing to push them to their limit. Should those limits be breached, the response will not be confined to the courts or the halls of Congress. Colombia has a long history of popular resistance to foreign interference, and any attempt to undermine its sovereignty will likely meet its strongest opposition in the streets, where the defense of national self-determination has so often been fought.
