articles.title: Bryan Stevenson: America Cannot Repair Racial Injustice Until It Confronts the Lies That Sustain It
articles.author: Sharon Kyle
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Civil War ended slavery, but it did not end the ideas that made slavery possible. That distinction, according to civil rights attorney Bryan Stevenson, helps explain why racial injustice has remained a permanent fixture in American institutions long after the abolition of slavery, the end of Jim Crow, and the victories of the civil rights movement. Speaking with California Governor Gavin Newsom in Montgomery, Alabama, Stevenson offered an analysis of American history that challenges conventional accounts of racial progress. The country's central failure, he argued, has not simply been its unwillingness to acknowledge particular atrocities. It has been its refusal to confront the ideology that justified those atrocities and continues to shape American political life. "I often argue that the north won the Civil War, but the south won the narrative war because those ideas of racial hierarchy prevailed," Stevenson said. That observation captures the central argument of their conversation: Political and legal victories cannot produce lasting racial justice when the beliefs that legitimized oppression remain intact. The Narrative That Survived Emancipation Stevenson, founder of the Equal Justice Initiative, has spent decades challenging wrongful convictions, excessive punishment, racial discrimination, and the treatment of children in America's criminal legal system. His work has convinced him that the most enduring legacy of enslavement was not confined to forced labor or the physical brutality of bondage. "I think the great evil, the enduring evil was the narrative that was created to justify enslavement," he told Newsom. Enslavers needed a moral framework that gave them a justification to continue to regard themselves as decent people even while kidnapping, buying and selling human beings, separating parents from children, and extracting wealth through violence and torture. That framework was the fabricated belief that Black people were inherently inferior to white people. The ideology was essential to the system. Without it, the exploitation of millions of enslaved people would have been much harder to reconcile personally and to reconcile with the nation's professed commitments to liberty, equality, and justice. While it is true that the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery, except as punishment for crime and the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments promised equal protection and voting rights, those constitutional changes did not eliminate the racial ideology that sustained the institution for generations. With the ideology remaining intact after the abolition of slavery, it simply adapted. After Reconstruction, Southern governments institutionalized racial segregation, disenfranchisement, and racial terror. Courts repeatedly failed to enforce the constitutional protections supposedly guaranteed to formerly enslaved people. The narrative of Black inferiority survived because the nation never undertook the sustained work of dismantling that ideology -- an ideology that exists today. Stevenson sees that failure as a defining feature of American history. The Politics of Fear and Anger The interview took place against the backdrop of renewed political attacks on immigrants, racial minorities, and efforts to teach the history of racism. Stevenson warned that political leaders who mobilize populations through fear and anger are drawing upon a dangerous historical tradition. He cited Nazi Germany and the Rwandan genocide as examples of what can happen when leaders encourage populations to regard identifiable groups as threatening, dangerous, or less than human. In the United States, he sees similar mechanisms operating through narratives that portray marginalized communities as criminal, undeserving, or threatening to the nation's identity. Those narratives can become particularly effective during periods of social and economic uncertainty. Racial resentment offers a political explanation for people's frustrations while directing their anger toward groups that often have relatively little institutional power. Stevenson described racial injustice as a form of inherited pollution. "I've long believed that the history of racial injustice in this country has created these toxins in the air. It's like pollution. We all breathe it in." The metaphor is instructive. Pollution does not require every person breathing contaminated air to have personally created the contamination. Its consequences extend across generations. Likewise, the effects of racial hierarchy persist through institutions, inherited assumptions, public policy, and political language—even among people who reject overt expressions of racial hatred. The danger, Stevenson suggested, is that societies that refuse to acknowledge these influences remain susceptible to leaders who know how to exploit them. Why Truth Must Come Before Repair Newsom's conversation with Stevenson also addressed reparations and the responsibilities of institutions that profited from enslavement and subsequent racial discrimination. In introducing the episode, Newsom described signing legislation requiring certain longstanding corporations to examine and publicly disclose historical connections to slavery. The examples included insurance policies written on enslaved people and financial transactions in which human beings were treated as collateral. Stevenson argued that meaningful repair requires an honest accounting of the harms committed. For him, truth-telling, accountability, reconciliation, and reparations are related but distinct stages of a larger process. "You've got to commit to truth-telling before you get to the beautiful R word," he explained. This is more than a moral appeal. Institutions cannot meaningfully repair harms they have not identified. Governments cannot design remedies without examining how past policies distributed wealth, opportunity, political power, and disadvantage. And the public cannot evaluate proposals for reparations without understanding what was taken, who benefited, and how those benefits and losses continue to shape the present. Stevenson pointed out that American society readily accepts financial compensation when contracts are violated or property rights are infringed. Yet demands for reparations following centuries of racial exploitation are frequently treated as unreasonable or divisive. The contrast reveals how differently the nation values injuries to property and injuries to human dignity. Repair, in this understanding, is not simply a matter of writing checks. It requires confronting the institutions and economic arrangements through which racial inequality was created and maintained. Remembering the History America Tried to Forget The setting for the conversation was particularly significant. Montgomery is home to the Equal Justice Initiative's Legacy Museum and National Memorial for Peace and Justice, which opened in 2018. These institutions document the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans, American enslavement, racial terror lynchings, segregation, and the connections between that history and mass incarceration. Stevenson described their purpose as filling a fundamental gap in American public memory. He compared the United States' treatment of its racial history with Germany's efforts to confront the Holocaust. German memorials, museums, educational requirements, and public markers make Nazi atrocities difficult to ignore. The United States, by contrast, has historically dedicated far more public space to celebrating powerful political and military figures than to remembering people who suffered under racial domination. Stevenson's point is not that remembering atrocities automatically prevents their recurrence. It is that deliberate public remembrance creates opportunities for education, acknowledgment, and accountability that collective silence cannot provide. His work in Montgomery demonstrates that confronting history need not remain an abstract intellectual exercise. Museums, memorials, historical markers, and documented personal stories can transform public understanding of events that have too often been omitted or misrepresented. The project also challenges communities beyond the South to recognize their own connections to racial exploitation. Enslavement was not exclusively a Southern institution. Northern ports, banks, insurance companies, and commercial enterprises also participated in and benefited from the economy of human bondage. A truthful national history must account for those connections. From Racial Terror to Mass Incarceration One of Stevenson's most consequential arguments concerns the connection between racial hierarchy and the American criminal legal system. The ideology that portrayed Black people as inherently inferior eventually evolved into narratives depicting them as inherently dangerous. Those narratives helped legitimize racial terror lynchings, discriminatory policing, harsh criminal sentencing, and policies that contributed to mass incarceration. Stevenson described the experience of representing clients who should have enjoyed the presumption of innocence but were instead presumed dangerous or guilty because of their race or poverty. He also recalled being threatened at gunpoint by police officers despite having graduated from Harvard Law School. His professional achievements did not insulate him from racial suspicion. The experience illustrates the limitations of approaches to racial inequality that emphasize individual educational attainment or economic advancement while neglecting systemic discrimination. Stevenson's broader point is that a society cannot understand mass incarceration without confronting the historical narratives that made extraordinary levels of punishment politically acceptable. During the late twentieth century, descriptions of young people as "super predators" helped justify increasingly punitive policies, including severe sentences imposed on children. Stevenson and the Equal Justice Initiative subsequently challenged such practices, securing major Supreme Court victories against mandatory life-without-parole sentences for children. He continues to question the moral legitimacy of the death penalty in a criminal legal system marked by racial discrimination, wrongful convictions, and unequal access to effective legal representation. For Stevenson, the central question about capital punishment is not simply whether a person convicted of a terrible crime deserves to die. It is whether a government operating through a profoundly imperfect system should exercise the power to kill. Hope Is Not the Same as Optimism Despite the weight of the history he described, Stevenson repeatedly returned to the necessity of hope. Newsom pressed him on how Americans should maintain hope amid political exhaustion, polarization, historical revisionism, and the continuing erosion of democratic norms. Stevenson's answer rejected the idea that hope depends on expecting circumstances to improve on their own. Hope is a discipline that creates obligations. He described an enslaved great-grandfather who risked punishment to learn to read and write when doing so was prohibited. After emancipation, that ancestor read newspapers aloud to formerly enslaved neighbors who had been denied literacy. Stevenson's grandmother inherited that commitment to education, eventually passing it to her children and grandchildren. Although she worked as a domestic worker throughout her life, she insisted that education could open possibilities for future generations. Stevenson remembered that his mother purchased a set of encyclopedias for the family even though doing so required taking on debt. He had never met a lawyer before attending Harvard Law School. Yet his family's insistence on learning helped make that future imaginable. Those experiences shaped his conviction that people have a responsibility to continue struggles whose outcomes they may never personally witness. "I just think it's what we owe our children. It's what we owe the future," he said. The distinction matters. Optimism can become an expectation that progress is inevitable. Hope, as Stevenson describes it, demands action even when progress appears uncertain. It is the conviction that people must struggle for a more just society because the alternative is to surrender that society's future to those most willing to exploit fear and division. The Work of Changing the American Story Perhaps the most important lesson of the conversation is that changing laws without changing public consciousness leaves the foundations of injustice vulnerable to reconstruction. Stevenson pointed to changes in public attitudes toward smoking and drunk driving as examples of how new information, sustained advocacy, and powerful personal narratives can transform social behavior and eventually public policy. He believes a similar transformation is necessary in America's understanding of racial injustice. "Learning is an action item," he insisted. But learning must be followed by participation. His emphasis on proximity—the importance of bringing people closer to the experiences of those who are marginalized—challenges the political and social arrangements that allow privilege to remain insulated from suffering. It also offers a response to the temptation to withdraw from civic engagement when conditions become overwhelming. At the conclusion of the conversation, Stevenson recalled a particularly difficult moment after an unsuccessful resentencing hearing for a client who had originally received life without parole as a child. Exhausted and discouraged, he stopped at a restaurant. A group of older Black women recognized him. One called him over, instructed him to bend down, kissed him on the forehead, and offered a simple instruction: "You keep on keeping on." The encounter reminded him that movements for justice are sustained not only by landmark court decisions and prominent leaders, but by ordinary people who recognize the importance of the struggle and encourage those carrying it forward. That understanding connects Stevenson's personal history with his institutional work and political analysis. The struggle for racial justice is also a struggle over what Americans are willing to remember, what they are prepared to acknowledge, and what kind of future they believe they have an obligation to create. The Civil War ended the legal institution of slavery. The civil rights movement dismantled much of the formal architecture of Jim Crow. But neither achievement fully defeated the narrative of racial hierarchy. Stevenson's message is that the next stage of American democracy must confront that unfinished work. Truth must become a public responsibility. Accountability must extend to institutions that benefited from racial exploitation. Repair must address the consequences of historical injustice. And hope must be translated into sustained collective action. Without those commitments, the nation risks continuing a familiar pattern: condemning the most visible manifestations of racial oppression while preserving the conditions that allow them to return in new forms. America's future, Stevenson suggests, depends on whether the country can finally replace the lies that justified racial domination with a more truthful understanding of its history—and a more expansive commitment to justice.

articles.title: Palestinians Face Down the Israeli Genocid
articles.author: Ramzy Baroud, Robert Corsini, Dick Price, Sharon Kyle
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On October 3, 2026, Palestinian American journalist, author, and historian Ramzy Baroud delivered a powerful keynote address at the Fourth Annual Left Coast Forum at California State University, Los Angeles. Speaking about Israel's genocide in Gaza and the Palestinian struggle for liberation, Baroud combined family history, anti-colonial analysis, and an urgent call for international solidarity. His central message was unmistakable: Palestinians are not simply victims of history. They are active participants in shaping it, and their refusal to disappear represents a fundamental challenge to the colonial system seeking to displace them. Ramzy Baroud: Left Coast Forum (49:29) A Sister's Life and Death Baroud began not with political theory but with the story of his sister, Dr. Suma Baroud, a physician who spent three decades delivering babies and treating the wounded in Gaza. After briefly leaving Gaza for Turkey, she returned voluntarily, compelled by her connection to her homeland and her responsibility to its people. During Israel's bombardment, she worked under devastating conditions, treating injured children without adequate electricity, medical supplies, or painkillers. In 2024, Baroud told the audience, an Israeli drone struck her vehicle as she returned from the hospital, killing her. Her story framed the central questions of his address: "Why do we stay? Why do we resist? Why do we refuse to disappear?" For Baroud, his sister's decision to remain in Gaza embodied a collective Palestinian commitment to land, community, and identity, even when remaining could mean death. Related: Beyond Israeli Apartheid: Why Britain's Greens Are Challenging Zionism Itself The Nakba Never Ended Baroud rejected the prevailing tendency to treat the destruction of Gaza as an isolated humanitarian catastrophe. Instead, he situated the current genocide within the historical continuum of the Nakba, the mass displacement and dispossession of Palestinians beginning in 1948. "The Nakba is an ongoing structural process," he declared. He traced this process through the expulsion of Palestinians from their villages, Israel's 1967 occupation, the Oslo agreements, and the prolonged siege of Gaza. Drawing on the 1923 writings of Zionist leader Ze'ev Jabotinsky, Baroud described the Iron Wall doctrine: the belief that overwhelming military superiority could eventually convince Palestinians that resistance was futile. Yet, he argued, decades of military domination have failed to extinguish Palestinian demands for freedom and self-determination. Baroud described the events beginning in October 2023 as a historic rupture that exposed the limits of military power. Whatever one's interpretation of October 7, he insisted that Palestinians must be recognized as people possessing political agency rather than merely as passive subjects of Israeli decisions. Reclaiming Palestinian History One of Baroud's strongest arguments concerned who gets to tell the Palestinian story. For generations, he observed, Palestinians have been described by colonial administrators, Western journalists, Israeli officials, and outside commentators whose interpretations frequently displaced Palestinian testimony. Even sympathetic solidarity movements have sometimes elevated outside voices over those of Palestinians themselves. Baroud called for what he termed "narrative sovereignty" : the right of Palestinians to document, interpret, and communicate their own history. He illustrated this through his family's experience. His parents came from a peasant community displaced from the village of Bayt Daras in 1948. Forced into refugee life in Gaza, they possessed few material resources, but his father insisted that education would become the family's source of strength. His sister eventually became a physician. For Baroud, such accounts are not simply family memories. They constitute a people's history that challenges attempts to erase Palestinian existence. He urged the audience to recognize the historical significance of refugees' testimonies, family photographs, village memories, and keys to homes from which Palestinians were expelled. Related: Israel Is Losing Hollywood Sumud: Survival as Resistance Baroud devoted particular attention to the Palestinian concept of sumud , commonly translated as steadfastness. But steadfastness, he explained, should not be confused with passive endurance. "Sumud is an active revolutionary strategy for survival and resistance," he said. He offered examples: a farmer replanting an uprooted olive tree, a teacher continuing lessons in a makeshift classroom, a family erecting a tent on the ruins of its destroyed home, and a doctor treating wounded patients without anesthesia. These actions, he argued, directly challenge a system that depends upon Palestinian displacement and disappearance. Drawing on Italian Marxist Antonio Gramsci's concept of organic intellectuals, Baroud also described Gaza's teachers, journalists, physicians, and mothers as individuals whose everyday work embodies political resistance. Their contributions deserve recognition alongside those of prominent political leaders and intellectuals. From Sympathy to Solidarity Turning to the international response, Baroud condemned Western governments for providing military, financial, and diplomatic support to Israel while professing commitments to human rights and international law. He contrasted those governments with the growing international movement demanding Palestinian freedom. He praised South Africa's decision to bring its genocide case against Israel before the International Court of Justice, alongside solidarity efforts across Africa, Latin America, and Europe. He also highlighted university encampments, labor organizing, weapons-factory protests, and dockworkers refusing to handle military cargo destined for Israel. For Baroud, these actions demonstrate the difference between expressions of sympathy and meaningful solidarity. Solidarity, he argued, requires shared risks and collective action. He connected Palestine's liberation struggle to the broader movements against colonialism, apartheid, and white supremacy, invoking thinkers including Frantz Fanon, James Baldwin, Malcolm X, and Angela Davis. Related: Iran War Exposing Limits of U.S. Power Building a Movement Around Principles Baroud concluded by challenging solidarity organizations to move beyond factional disputes and disagreements over political personalities. Movements, he maintained, must organize around enduring principles rather than individual leaders. Among those principles he identified were Palestinian self-determination, racial and economic equality, the right of refugees to return, and an end to settler-colonial apartheid. He also rejected approaches that focus exclusively on humanitarian relief while leaving the structures responsible for Palestinian dispossession intact. "We must stop managing the victims and start confronting the system of oppression," he told the audience. His closing challenge shifted responsibility from Palestinians, whose steadfastness he considered established, to those watching from abroad. "The question is, what will we do?" It was a fitting conclusion to an address grounded in both tragedy and determination. Baroud asked his listeners not merely to witness Palestinian suffering, but to recognize Palestinian agency and accept responsibility for translating solidarity into organized political power. For the Left Coast Forum audience, his message reached beyond Gaza: liberation requires more than sympathy for the oppressed. It demands confronting the systems that produce oppression—and joining the struggles of those determined to overcome them. Rob Corsini of Videocratic Media recorded and created the video.

articles.title: Rubber Bullets
articles.author: Cerise Castle
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Tucker Collins, 19, has undergone a series of changes since last year. He started his freshman year as an astronautical engineering student at the University of Southern California. He moved to a new part of Los Angeles. And on March 28, he lost an eye from an injury sustained at a protest against federal immigration enforcement. That afternoon, the amateur photographer and filmmaker decided to go to a No Kings protest in downtown Los Angeles with a new camera his parents gave him as a Christmas gift, he told Capital & Main. He was there to film and photograph Department of Homeland Security agents who have carried out a series of aggressive immigration raids under President Donald Trump. ”I think we’ve seen with DHS specifically, in this case, being used, weaponized into a force of terror against everyday citizens,” he said. “I was there to document any potential crimes.” Collins was walking as part of a large group of protesters, holding up his camera toward DHS agents near the Metropolitan Detention Center, a prison in downtown L.A. used to detain immigrants, when he was hit in the face with a kinetic impact projectile — also known as a less-lethal round — according to video taken by another protester and provided to Capital & Main by Collins’ attorney V. James DeSimone. Collins crumpled to the ground and began to scream, the video showed, and strangers pulled him to safety. Another protester drove him to the hospital, he said, and the injuries were so severe that his eye had to be surgically removed. Collins is soft-spoken with long blond hair covering the right side of his face. When he moves, his hair sweeps away just long enough to reveal a large black eye patch covering a glass eye underneath. “This was a crime, and it was, I guess, surprising that it happened to me,” he said. “But not surprising that it happened.” Tucker Collins and his glass eye. Photo by Ben Camacho for Capital & Main. Collins is one of numerous people injured by local police or federal agents during protests that have continued in Southern California in the year following the Trump administration’s surge of immigration enforcement actions that began in June 2025. In dozens of cases, local and federal officers, often outfitted in riot helmets and bulletproof vests, have fired kinetic impact projectiles, including plastic or rubber bullets commonly referred to as less-lethal rounds, into crowds of demonstrators. Los Angeles Police Department officers fired at least 2,587 such rounds at protesters between June 6, 2025, and March 28, 2026, according to use-of-force reports published by the department. While there is no official tally of the number of people injured during protests in Southern California, the Los Angeles Press Club has documented in a federal lawsuit over a dozen incidents in which journalists in the area were injured covering the protests. Some of the people injured recovered in the days and weeks after, but others were left with life-altering wounds. Those with serious injuries have filed claims or lawsuits against police or federal law enforcement. A Capital & Main review of claims and lawsuits filed since June 2025, as well as interviews with attorneys and reviews of bystander videos, documented at least five people who were, like Collins, shot in the eye with a projectile. Capital & Main spoke with three of them, each of whom described feeling anxiety and a sense that something deeply unjust had happened to them. They said they were also continuing to reckon with their lives being suddenly and permanently altered. Related: Civil Rights and the Billion Dollar Price Tag Taxpayers Pay Instead All of the five injured men lost vision in at least one eye. Three of them required surgeries to remove their injured eyes, according to legal claims filed against the agencies whose officers they believed to be responsible. Each of them has had to navigate the new challenges of living with a significant visual impairment. The Los Angeles Police Department and U.S. Department of Homeland Security did not respond to Capital & Main’s questions about the complaints filed against them by five people who were shot in the eye. The agencies have said elsewhere that they do not keep internal records of the total number of injuries to protesters since June 2025. Lost Forever Due to the severity of his injury, Collins was transferred to another hospital where a surgeon removed five plastic fragments of a projectile from his skull, said Collins and his attorney, V. James DeSimone. The fragments destroyed the structure of Collins’ eye. And the collection of blood and fluid that made up the remains of his eye were determined to have passed the point of repair, they said, so the eye was removed. The first few weeks of his recovery were filled with agonizing headaches, Collins said. “The pain was still too much for me to want to do anything but lie in bed all day,” he said. “It hurt to move my head.” Since losing his eye, Collins said he has had to relearn dozens of basic tasks, from walking without running into people and objects to completing his schoolwork. Collins takes a selfie in the hospital while being treated for his eye injury. “I’m worried how much it will, you know, impact my ability to do the things I love,” he said. “I’d like to think that I’ll still be able to do my career path as normal, but in reality I don’t know.” Marcos Lemor, an ophthalmologist affiliated with Adventist Health-White Memorial and East Los Angeles Doctors Hospital who surgically removed what was left of Collins’ eye, said that the gravity of his injury presented a significant challenge. Without both eyes, Collins has lost his depth perception. “He’s never going to be able to really do that kind of very fine manual work because he does not have that perception,” Lemor said, “That’s lost forever.” Collins is still grappling with his new reality and said he feels a great sense of loss. “It’s strange to think of my life now having a before and after,” Collins said. Lives Changed Collins isn’t the only protester or bystander to sustain a life-altering eye injury from a law enforcement projectile at a Southern California protest. During a previous No Kings rally on June 16, 2025, an LAPD officer shot photographer Marshall Woodruff, 29, in his right eye, according to a lawsuit filed against the department. His eye had to be removed, leaving the aspiring filmmaker with an uncertain future in film, said his attorney, Aaron Liskin, a partner at Kinsella Holley Iser Kump Steinsapir LLP in Los Angeles. Homeland Security agents shot both college student Kaden Rummler, 21, and visual artist Britain Rodriguez, 31, in the face during a protest outside Santa Ana City Hall on Jan. 9. Video captured an agent in body armor dragging Rummler by the collar of his hoodie, covered in blood. Both Rodriguez and Rummler were hit in the eye, according to claims they filed against the Department of Homeland Security. Each of them later had to have an eye removed. Rummler was initially charged with felony assault on a federal agent. His charge has since been reduced to an infraction of “creating a hazard on federal property.” He paid a fine of $250 and a $30 processing fee, according to federal court documents reviewed by Capital & Main. Jesus Javier Gomez Islas, 23, was riding a scooter home from work near a demonstration at the Metropolitan Detention Center on Jan. 31 when he was shot in the eye by a Los Angeles Police Department officer, according to his attorney, Jamal Tooson, a partner at Lessem, Newstat & Tooson, LLP in Los Angeles, and a claim filed by Gomez Islas against the department. Gomez Islas had his eye surgically removed, according to Tooson and the filing. Related: Racist and Sexist Remarks Agents in ICE Shootings Made Tooson said that his client has developed sympathetic ophthalmia, a rare, auto-immune condition that occurs when the inner eye tissue is exposed and the body does not recognize it as its own. The immune system then launches an attack to destroy the healthy eye. He said Gomez Islas is in danger of losing his remaining eye due to the severity of the original injury. In an email, a Los Angeles Police Department spokesperson Norma Eisenman declined to respond to questions about Gomez Islas’ cases because it is “pending litigation.” In July, then-spokesperson Department of Homeland Security spokesperson Lauren Bis did not answer questions about Rummler’s, Rodriguez’s and Collins’ injuries or its practices, but sent a statement saying, “We remind the public that rioting is dangerous — obstructing law enforcement is a federal crime and assaulting law enforcement is a felony.” The statement also included the following statement in response to questions about photographers and reporters injured while covering protests. “We remind members of the media to exercise caution as they cover these violent riots and remind journalists that covering unlawful activities in the field does come with risks — though our officers take every reasonable precaution to mitigate those dangers to those exercising protected First Amendment rights.” Undeterred Collins said he is resolute in his commitment to return to a normal life. He dreams of being an astronautical engineer; he wants to build rockets that go into outer space. A few weeks after he was discharged from the hospital, he joined USC’s Rocket Propulsion Lab in Nevada’s Black Rock Desert for a launch. He has been able to stay engaged in the field with the help of the university’s rocketry team for now. That kind of precision work is “so much harder now that I have one eye,” Collins said. But Collins said his experience has left him more confident in the importance of documenting what he sees. He plans to pick up his camera again and return to protests to bear witness. Capital & Main

articles.title: Considerations for the Utah 2026 General Election
articles.author: Democratic Socialists of Salt Lake
articles.content: This post is a shared statement by Salt Lake DSA’s Electoral Working Group explaining how we’re thinking about the upcoming election in Utah. Introduction The 2026 general election is fast approaching, and once again the working class faces a crucial question: how should we participate in an electoral system structured to disempower us? As always, voting is neither the beginning nor the end of politics. Building a better future requires building collective power to take action and affect the conditions of our lives year-round. Nevertheless, voting plays a distinct and important role in expanding our capacity to organize and advance the socialist movement. Our enemies understand this. The far-right Trump regime has continually sought to undermine elections , threaten voters , and attack left-wing elected officials , while tech oligarchs increasingly openly oppose democracy itself. Salt Lake DSA (SLDSA) is committed to protecting the right to vote, and as part of that commitment, we will participate in the No Kings: Vote Early! rallies in Salt Lake City and Ogden on Saturday, Oct.17. We encourage all SLDSA members and fellow comrades to show up and demonstrate that we will not be intimidated by the Trump regime’s attack on our voting rights! That said, SLDSA’s Electoral Working Group is not endorsing or recommending any specific candidates in Utah elections this year. We are, however, recommending how to vote on this year’s proposed constitutional amendments and offering guidance on what socialists should consider when evaluating candidates. Constitutional Amendments Two proposed constitutional amendments are up for consideration: Amendment A and Amendment B . The Utah State Legislature, dominated by landlords and developers, has put forth both amendments amid the ongoing fight over the Proposition 4 Redistricting Initiative . Together, they give the legislature more power while making it harder to pass citizen-proposed initiatives, which Utah workers have historically used to create better organizing conditions. For this reason, SLDSA’s Electoral Working Group recommends voting AGAINST both constitutional amendments. Amendment A “Shall the Utah Constitution be amended to change how proposed constitutional amendments are published, requiring publication for 60 days immediately before the general election in a manner established by state law instead of in newspapers?” SLDSA’s Electoral Working Group recommends voting AGAINST Amendment A. Amendment A strips essential checks and balances on the legislature’s power to amend Utah’s constitution. If passed, this amendment would remove a long-standing provision requiring the legislature to publish all proposed constitutional amendments publicly, specifically in newspapers, at least two months before Election Day, and would let the legislature set its own rules for proposing constitutional amendments and notify the public only as it sees fit. This is only the latest entry in the Utah legislature’s long history of trying to deny working-class participation in the democratic process. Year after year, the legislature has proven that it will always take the opportunity to set rules that increase its own power at our expense . The History of Amendment A is a Lesson in Organizing In 2024, the Utah State Legislature attempted to place two misleadingly worded constitutional amendments on the ballot at the last minute: 2024’s Amendment D would have allowed the legislature to rescind Proposition 4’s redistricting requirements despite it being approved by voters and later upheld by the Utah Supreme Court. 2024’s Amendment A would have allowed the legislature to redirect income taxes away from education and services for people with disabilities and towards other legislative priorities. The directionality here is instructive: both of these measures were designed to shift power away from voters and workers and toward the reactionary legislature . Because the legislature proposed both initiatives at the 11th hour, overriding statutory safeguards to ensure they appeared on the 2024 general election ballot, it neglected to publish the initiatives to newspapers statewide, violating the mandatory notice requirement . In response, the Utah Education Association and the League of Women Voters successfully sued to remove both amendments from the ballot. In retaliation for a teachers union successfully standing up to its attempt to seize power, the legislature passed HB 267 attempting to eradicate the ability of all public unions in Utah to bargain collectively. The sponsor of the bill, Jordan Teuscher, who is also an executive in the LDS Church’s business arm, posted an op-ed in the Wall Street Journal airing his grievances with public unions in general (a broadside which earned him a $15,000 check from “school choice” real-estate investor Howard Rich ). The story doesn’t end there. Throughout the spring of 2025, Utah Unions and community organizers formed the Protect Utah Workers Coalition , which gathered more than 250,000 signatures to put forward a ballot measure to overturn HB 267. Rather than face an embarrassing defeat at the ballot box, the Utah legislature repealed its own bill in December 2025 . This saga offers an important lesson for socialist organizers: the Utah legislature is a power center that is structurally and personally opposed to workers’ interests. Any power given to it will be used to attack our ability to organize collectively. Allowing it to set the terms for publishing constitutional amendments can only undermine our position. Amendment B “Shall the Utah Constitution be amended to require that citizen-proposed laws that increase taxes compared to existing law be approved by at least 60% of voters, instead of a simple majority?” SLDSA’s Electoral Working Group recommends voting AGAINST Amendment B. Amendment B directly attacks our ability to organize for better policies through the ballot initiative process. If passed, this amendment would raise the bar for passing initiatives that increase taxes from 50% (a simple majority) to 60%. The legislature defines initiatives that “ increase taxes ” as creating new taxes, expanding existing taxes, or raising existing tax rates. This definition, combined with the increased pass threshold, effectively eliminates our ability to organize for policies that redistribute wealth and fund public goods and services. Citizen-led ballot initiatives in Utah are a crucial tool for workers to create better organizing conditions. Escalating attempts to undermine the referendum process only reaffirm its importance in challenging the power of the oligarch-aligned Utah Legislature. Like workers everywhere, we understand how frustrating it is to see our taxes go toward unjust causes and wasteful advertising campaigns . However, we still believe it needs to be made easier, not harder, to organize for policies that actually meet the needs of the working class, especially policies that increase taxes to fund material change. Candidates SLDSA remains focused on empowering workers and running candidates that our members democratically choose to represent our chapter’s socialist values. We don’t believe that change is held in the hands of politicians, or that voting alone can fix the everyday challenges we face. Instead, we believe an organized working class and collective action are the only means to enact real, systemic change. As such, we offer no endorsements or recommendations of specific candidates for any 2026 Utah general election race . Nevertheless, we recognize voting as an important tool for creating conditions that make it easier for us to organize. We encourage everyone to vote in their local races and consider issues raised in DSA’s Workers Deserve More program when deciding who to vote for. SLDSA, in particular, is focused on our campaigns to protect our communities from ICE and to protect our ability to organize by forming the Coalition to Defend Freedom of Speech and Democratic Rights . As you fill out your ballot, we invite you to consider whether the candidates you vote for have demonstrated the moral and structural fortitude to take on ICE and whether they have taken actions that expand and protect our ability to organize or actions that undermine it. The post Considerations for the Utah 2026 General Election first appeared on Salt Lake DSA .

articles.title: UAW President Shawn Fain, International Executive Board Sworn In for New Four-Year Term
articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content: United Auto Workers (UAW) President Shawn Fain and the union’s newly elected International Executive Board (IEB) were sworn into office for a new four-year term in a ceremony honoring the will of the membership and reaffirming the union’s commitment to fighting for its members and all working-class people. Press is encouraged to use photos from the swearing-in ceremony . The ceremony marked the beginning of a new term for Fain and the International Executive Board, who pledged to faithfully serve the union’s membership and advance the interests of UAW members, families, and their communities. UAW member and longtime union leader Paul Caucci administered the oath of office to Fain, who begins his second term as International Union president. Fain then administered the constitutional obligation to the newly elected members of the International Executive Board. In remarks following the ceremony, Fain reflected on the responsibility of union leadership and outlined the priorities for the next four years: growing the UAW, building worker power and winning improvements for working-class people. Fain connected the UAW’s history of collective action to the challenges facing workers today, pointing to the legacy of the 1930s sit-down strikes and the union’s more recent Stand Up Strike in 2023. “Our union built the American Dream,” Fain said. “From the Sit Down Strikers of the 1930’s to the Stand-Up Strikers since 2023, regular working-class people have led this union and led this country from the ground up.” “Over the next four years, our job is to do more than just to ensure the survival of our organization,” Fain said. “We need to grow. We need to build. We need to win. And to do that, we need each other.” Fain emphasized that the UAW is a democratic, member-driven organization and that the union’s future depends on members being prepared and empowered to fight for their interests. “This is a democracy,” Fain said. “We are only in this room because the members put us in this room. And we will only win what the members are prepared and empowered to fight for.” The president also highlighted the broader stakes of the labor movement, citing wealth inequality and the influence of corporate power as challenges facing working people. He urged UAW leaders to meet those challenges through faith, solidarity and collective action. “The only path to turning this situation around is by abandoning fear and having faith that’s rooted in solidarity,” Fain said. Fain closed his remarks by calling on the board to approach the next four years with a shared sense of purpose and responsibility. “It’s not our individual legacies on the line. It’s not just our union on the line,” Fain said. “It’s the fate of the working class and the fate of humanity.” “And together, we will rise to the occasion—to meet our generation’s defining moment. And we will do it as a United UAW.” Newly Sworn-In UAW International Executive Board The International Executive Board members sworn into office alongside President Fain are: President: Shawn Fain Secretary-Treasurer: Brandon Campbell Vice President: Laura Dickerson Vice President: Kevin Gotinsky Vice President: Ryan Hiestand Region 1 Director: LaShawn English Region 1A Director: Mark DePaoli Region 1D Director: Scott Zuckschwerdt Region 2B Director: David Green Region 4 Director: Lucas DeSpain Region 6 Director: Mike Miller Region 8 Director: Tim Smith Region 9 Director: Jimmy Lakeman Region 9A Director: Brandon Mancilla The UAW enters its new term focused on expanding the union’s reach through a $100 million investment in new organizing, building worker power and fighting for a better future for workers and their families. As growing wealth inequality threatens the foundations of democracy, the union will confront the challenges and opportunities posed by artificial intelligence and automation, fight for a new trade policy that puts workers first, and fight for a political system that puts workers at the center. The focus of this work will remain the UAW’s core priorities: higher wages, quality health care, retirement security and more time off the job.

articles.title: Economics News for Workers, October 2026
articles.content: On September 16, the Federal Reserve Board raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percent, the first rate hike in three years. Minutes from the meeting which were released in early October indicate that the board of governors expects to impose another rate increase before the end of the year. They meet again on October 28 and December 9. The rate increase, while justified as a means to fight inflation, was primarily meant to reassure international financial markets that the U.S. will make good on its debt, which has spiraled due to the combination of tax cuts for the wealthy and military spending. Higher interest rates are essentially a tax imposed on working people, who will pay higher rates on credit cards and mortgages while also bearing the brunt of slower job growth. (When interest rates are higher, it is more expensive for businesses to borrow money, and they are less likely to expand and hire new workers.) Rising Energy Prices Erase All Wage Gains Since Trump’s Inauguration New data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ September jobs report and Consumer Price Index numbers shows that over the past year, inflation has increased by 3.7 percent, while hourly wage rate increases have fallen to only three percent. This means that the average American worker has seen a 0.7 percent real decline in the value of their wages since September 2025. Or, to put it another way, there has been no net increase in real wages since Trump took office in January, 2025. McDonald’s Using AI to Gouge Consumers In another sign that mature businesses will attempt any tactic to maximize profit, fast food company McDonald’s is now using dynamic pricing based on AI-gathered information. Algorithms track sales across 14,000 restaurants and bring in outside data, such as publicly-posted prices by competitors, to determine how much locals are willing to pay for an item on the menu. A recent article in Reuters notes that comparing two restaurants two miles apart, one is selling a Big Mac for a 21 percent markup over the second. Dynamic pricing has become commonly used by online retailers and rideshare apps like Uber, but the expansion into brick-and-mortar retail is a relatively recent dynamic. Water Bills Up 62 Percent in Last Decade A new study by Food & Water Watch has found that water bills for U.S. households have increased by 62 percent over the past ten years. By comparison, food prices have increased by 30 percent and overall consumer prices by 39 percent in the same period. “Corporate water abuses, federal disinvestment and climate change are supercharging water rate hikes across the country,” said study co-author Mary Grant, the water program director at Food & Water Watch. “Corporate control of water systems exacerbates this affordability crisis, as big water monopolies take away local control, prioritize profit and hike water prices even higher.” The study found that corporate-owner, for-profit water companies charged, on average, 67 percent higher rates than publicly-owned systems. Damaging New Rules on Student Loans Take Effect A new Education Department rule finalized in September means that for the first time, the government will judge eligibility for student loans based upon the “earnings potential” of graduates of the program. Essentially, the department will now look at the average earnings of graduates of a major or degree. If, for example, graduates of a particular bachelor's program make less on average than those with only a high school diploma, the program will be ineligible for federal loans. A defense of the new rule published earlier this year by an American Enterprise Institute fellow who was one of its architects noted the bulk of impacted students were enrolled in “undergraduate certificates” (often at for-profit institutions) in areas like cosmetology and massage therapy, occupations that required no educational background prior to the last few decades of degree inflation. However, the author’s own study also notes that almost two thirds of Master’s degrees in areas like social work and mental health fail to meet the earnings threshold, as the average graduate makes less money than the median worker with just a college degree. Given the pervasive underfunding of social and mental health services, it’s unlikely that the pay scale of these degrees will improve, meaning a critical shortage of new workers in these fields is the most likely outcome. Scammers Rob SNAP Recipients While Trump Administration Does Little to Stop Them Propublica has published an expose on the growing issue of food stamp theft. This is not the theft fearmongered about in right-wing media — recipients using food stamps towards improper purchases — but organized theft of SNAP benefits from recipients . In 2025,this totalled $470 million in benefits, with nearly one million households having had some money stolen. Typically this happens when the mag-stripe information on a card is intercepted (often due to purchases at a disreputable store), with a third party draining the account by purchasing large amounts of baby formula, energy drinks, or other valid SNAP purchase. The thief then resells the purchased product for profit. The most outrageous aspect of this SNAP theft is it would be easy to solve if electronic benefit transfer cards integrated the same sort of chip technology now otherwise universal for credit and debit cards. Indeed, a handful of states, including California, have introduced said cards (which in the case of California, reduced SNAP theft by 83 percent). However, cuts to SNAP funding under the “One Big Beautiful Bill” mean that the vast majority of states are blocked from implementing similar programs. In addition, 2025 cuts made by Elon Musk’s short-lived but highly destructive “Department of Government Oversight” have decimated the number of staff who oversee SNAP. Finally, Trump reversed a Biden-era policy which allowed for recipients to be reimbursed for stolen benefits, meaning that even in the rare cases these scammers are caught, no restitution is paid back to those who had to do without food assistance due to theft.

articles.title: Dattner’s Architects Say They Want a Union
articles.author: Alex N. Press
articles.content: On the west side of Manhattan, near the entrance to the Holland Tunnel, there is a nearly seventy-foot-tall concrete building containing five thousand tons of road salt. The walls of the Spring Street Salt Shed slope inward and outward in enormous pale planes; the whole thing is meant to resemble a grain of salt. Across the street stands a much larger garage that accommodates more than 150 sanitation vehicles, its long facades covered in glass and aluminum louvers. The two buildings were designed together, an attempt to make a sprawling sanitation facility fit into a residential neighborhood where residents had initially fought its construction. Writing about the complex in 2016, Architectural Record called the shed “as compelling as many pieces of public art in Manhattan.” The Salt Shed is a Dattner Architects project, designed with WXY Architecture + Urban Design. So are the 34th Street–Hudson Yards subway station, the Bronx Library Center, parts of Hudson River Park, Riverbank State Park, and thousands of units of housing around New York. Richard Dattner founded the firm in 1964, and public architecture and infrastructure have been central to its work ever since. Now the more than one hundred workers at Dattner are taking an unusual step in their industry: organizing with the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM). The proposed wall-to-wall bargaining unit includes designers, architects, and operations staff across the firm, excluding management and certain other positions. Organizers say they have support from a supermajority of workers. On October 21, Dattner workers will gather at city hall for a listening session with Deputy Mayor Julie Su to discuss the union effort. The meeting comes as workers are pressing the firm’s partners to agree to a process for recognizing their union without a National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) election. “The City has long worked alongside union employers, and we’ve seen the value that worker voice brings to public projects,” said Cassio Mendoza, a spokesperson for Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “We support every worker’s free and fair choice on this question, and the decision belongs to them.” The campaign has been quietly underway for years, extending across Dattner’s three studios and among employees at different points in their careers. Building a supermajority at a firm of this size took time, particularly with workers coming to the campaign for different reasons. “Some might be personal or specific to the firm, while for others, it might be about broader concerns with the industry and previous experiences that they had,” a Dattner designer said. Three Dattner employees spoke to Jacobin for this story. We would ordinarily identify workers discussing their organizing efforts, but there have been allegations of retaliation against union supporters in the architecture industry in recent years. At the firm Snøhetta, eight employees lost their jobs shortly after a 2023 union election. The NLRB later accused the firm of firing them for their union activity. The case has yet to be resolved. We are withholding the Dattner employees’ names so they can speak freely about the campaign. Dattner is, by the accounts of the workers I spoke with, a relatively good place to work. A licensed architect at Dattner described it as a leader in working conditions within the industry. That makes its union campaign an opportunity to set a precedent. “If we don’t lead this effort, if a firm like ours just can’t or won’t lead this effort, who’s going to?” the architect asked. Dattner calls itself a mission-driven firm . Riverbank State Park puts a park atop a wastewater treatment plant; Via Verde, designed with Grimshaw, is a mixed-income housing development in the South Bronx; the 34th Street–Hudson Yards station was the first new subway station to open in the city in more than twenty-five years. Much of the firm’s work is commissioned by public agencies. “We’re trying to create in our work a more democratic city, more democratic spaces for people to live in,” the architect said. “If we want to make more democratic spaces, that starts in the office. And having a more democratic process in the office is only going to allow us to do our jobs better, fulfill our mission better.” The Work Behind the Buildings The architect is easy to imagine somewhere above the city, a kind of deity with the vision to change the landscape of a metropolis and the power to make everyone else go along: scores of people to build it, and the rest of us to live in it. A line on an architectural drawing can eventually become an instruction for many others to build something. But getting from that line to the building requires engineers, contractors, construction workers, clients, and public agencies, along with plenty of work inside the architecture firm itself. The work can mean navigating building codes and zoning rules, responding to clients, and producing and revising digital models and drawings. “There is drudge work,” an associate at Dattner said. “It’s not all drawing pictures and picking colors.” Becoming a licensed architect can take a long time, too. According to the National Council of Architectural Registration Boards, the average person who earned a license in 2025 took 12.3 years to get there, including their education. For all that education and training, architecture is not an especially lucrative profession for many of its practitioners. The profession nevertheless retains a powerful image of the architect as a singular creative genius, a Frank Lloyd Wright whose talent might eventually bring wealth and acclaim. For those who imagine they might someday join his ranks, long hours and modest pay can seem like dues worth paying. “There’s this culture of suffering for the work, of pouring yourself into it because it is this creative discipline,” the Dattner architect said. “I’ve been in situations before where we felt like we needed to explore another idea, we needed to explore another scheme, and it’s just not acceptable to say, ‘We don’t have time for that.’” Long hours are familiar to architects well before they enter the profession. Architecture students routinely spend nights in the studio, and the hours don’t necessarily improve once they’re employed. Firms compete for commissions, often on price, and employees can end up working nights and weekends to get projects finished. “I know many of my classmates who have already left the profession before they got licensed because it wasn’t sustainable for them,” the designer said. The cost of living in New York has made the profession’s pay harder to accept. “My rent costs more money, and I’m more exhausted than I’ve ever been in my life,” the Dattner associate said. “We were all sold this bill of goods: go to college, get educated, become a white-collar professional, and you’re going to have a good life,” said the Dattner architect: We love what we do. I do have a good life, and there are certainly many working-class people who are being squeezed much more. But between the affordability crisis, AI, and discussions of how things need to change in our industry that have been going on for the past decade, it has created a moment where folks like us see an opportunity. People who came before us fought for labor rights, fought for the ability to bargain, and now it’s our time to take up the charge. How Architects Started Organizing Architects have not traditionally thought of themselves as the sort of workers who form unions. But neither did many other white-collar professionals — including graduate students, journalists , and tech workers — who have been organizing in recent years. C. G. Beck, an architect and writer involved in organizing in the industry, welcomed the Dattner campaign. “Dattner’s unionization campaign is a step forward for all workers in our industry,” Beck said. Peggy Deamer, an architect and a founder of the Architecture Lobby , a grassroots organization advocating for better working conditions and unionization in the profession, has spent years urging architects to think of themselves as workers, with the same concerns about pay, hours, and working conditions as anyone else. Through its Architectural Workers United campaign, the IAM has been involved in a small wave of organizing efforts at New York City architecture firms, where private sector unionism had barely existed for generations. In 2021, workers at SHoP Architects filed for an NLRB election with the IAM. They withdrew the petition shortly before the scheduled vote after what the union described as a “powerful anti-union campaign.” In 2022, workers at Bernheimer Architecture took another route: the firm voluntarily recognized its union, the first union at a private sector American architecture firm in decades. The workers ratified a first contract in 2024, winning a thirty-six-hour workweek, compensatory time off for additional hours, and overtime pay after forty-five hours. Workers at Snøhetta voted thirty-five to twenty-nine against unionization in 2023. At Sage and Coombe Architects, workers won voluntary recognition that year and ratified a first contract this spring. Of those campaigns, the two that have reached a first contract were recognized voluntarily. At Dattner, workers have asked management to agree to a process for recognizing the union without an NLRB election. Under the proposed agreement, Dattner would remain neutral while a third party checked whether a majority of employees had signed union cards. The Fight for Recognition On September 23, workers sent Dattner’s partners a letter requesting a card-check neutrality agreement. Six days later, the partners circulated a response to employees, reviewed by Jacobin , calling the IAM’s approach “secretive” and arguing that union representation should be decided through an election, “just as the way we pick a mayor or senator.” Architecture firms have been struggling with a prolonged downturn. According to the American Institute of Architects, firms have reported declining billings for most of the past three and a half years. In August, firms in the Northeast reported their steepest decline since 2020. The partners, meanwhile, warned that unionization could cost Dattner clients, claiming that the small architecture firms where the IAM had won recognition “have not thrived in the wake of unionization and the employees do not seem to have benefitted.” They also claimed that once employees unionized, it would become illegal for management to make individualized accommodations for employees, although federal labor law does not categorically prohibit such arrangements. They further disputed the idea that collective bargaining would give workers a say in which projects the firm pursued or how it conducted business. Dattner’s management did not respond to a request for comment. The organizing committee sent a second letter on October 5. “We are not requesting voluntary recognition, nor an election agreement,” the workers wrote. “Considering the current federal administration, we believe that it would be best for everyone to find a process outside of the NLRB.” They also emphasized that they were not seeking a predetermined union contract. “Our contract is our own,” they wrote. They asked the partners to meet with their union representative and respond by Friday, October 9. In an email to staff on that date, Dattner management wrote that it did not believe card-check neutrality “would be in the best interest of Dattner Architects or our employees.” “Meet us at the table,” the Dattner associate said when asked what she would like to say to Dattner’s management. “We’re ready and excited to talk about the ways that we see this being beneficial, not just for the firm, but for something larger than ourselves.” If the union is recognized, the IAM says, Dattner would become the largest unionized architecture firm in the United States. Workers argued that unionization could help the firm retain employees and appeal to clients that share its commitments. They also hoped to have more influence over how the firm operates, including greater transparency around compensation. “We can’t see the books,” the Dattner associate said. “The office purports to have positive values, including equity, and they tell us that we have pay equity. But we can’t confirm that without really having a seat at the table.” “This is not a movement against anything,” she said. “It is a movement for something. There’s a lot of positive energy among the group about how working as architects doing important work for the city and beyond can be something that also includes a great quality of life and a great working experience.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: More Than Ball Fields
articles.author: Bill Gould
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. For generations of Altadena families, Charles S. Farnsworth Park has been much more than ballfields at the foot of the San Gabriel Mountains. It has been one of the places where Altadena comes together. Children learned to throw and catch there, parents watched from the stands, coaches became mentors and neighbors became friends. But Farnsworth has always served a broader community. Its playgrounds, tennis and pickleball courts and basketball courts provided recreation for all ages. The historic Davies Building and amphitheater hosted plays, concerts, voting and community celebrations. Farnsworth was not simply a park; it was part of Altadena’s civic life. As someone whose family lost our home and all of our belongings in the Eaton Fire, I have spent much of the past year thinking and writing about what genuine recovery should mean. I have argued that rebuilding must be centered on people and that survivors should not be left to navigate recovery alone. For many families, this process will take years. That is why rebuilding places like Farnsworth matters. Before the fire, I wrote about my family’s experience with baseball in Altadena. Our son grew up playing with Central Altadena Little League (C.A.L.L.) and the Altadena Baseball Academy, much of it at Farnsworth. I described the park as a “truly picturesque backdrop,” with the San Gabriel Mountains giving Altadena baseball a home-field advantage that had little to do with the scoreboard. Related: Rebuilding After the Eaton Fire: Disaster Recovery Isn’t Working. Here’s What Survivors Really Need The Eaton Fire devastated Altadena in January 2025, destroying thousands of homes and severely damaging Farnsworth. C.A.L.L. suddenly found itself without its longtime home. Yet baseball became one way Altadena refused to surrender its sense of community. That did not happen by accident. C.A.L.L.’s board and league leaders — many of whom lost homes or were displaced — made the remarkable decision to keep the league going. Working with coaches, parents, donors and neighboring leagues that offered fields, they put together a 2025 season and created some normalcy for children experiencing extraordinary disruption. That story became the documentary Going for Home. The Los Angeles Dodgers Foundation’s announcement that it will invest $1.4 million to restore two fields at Farnsworth therefore represents something larger than a sports construction project. Dodgers Dreamfields 69 and 70 will include improved playing surfaces and irrigation, fencing, shade structures, solar-powered scoreboards modeled after those at Dodger Stadium and a STEM Trail incorporating the foundation’s Science of Baseball curriculum. Groundbreaking is scheduled for Nov. 5. For Los Angeles Dodgers Foundation CEO Nichol McKenzie-Whiteman, the devastation gave the organization’s work a different meaning. “The Los Angeles Dodgers Foundation has been revitalizing baseball fields since 2003, but we’ve never had to restore fields due to events like the ones that occurred last year,” McKenzie-Whiteman said. “For me, it put our work in a new light; we’re restoring places that held deep sentimental value for generations of families who gathered and played in these parks.” Norma Garcia, Director of the County of Los Angeles Department of Parks and Recreation, asked the Dodgers Foundation to help with Altadena’s parks. Her department also raised $100,000 from DICK’S Sporting Goods to help pay for stands and shade — important additions for families spending hours at the fields. Garcia said the County has requested FEMA assistance for Farnsworth but, so far, has received no FEMA help for the park. Garcia described the new fields as representing “hope, healing, and renewed opportunities” for Altadena’s young people and families. For Matthew Milton, whose family has deep roots in C.A.L.L., the announcement carries special significance. “This is a blessing,” Milton said. “I’m glad the history of Jackie Robinson from this area has led the Dodgers Foundation to make this meaningful contribution to Altadena.” That connection is fitting. Jackie Robinson’s roots in the Pasadena-Altadena area are an important part of the region’s African American history. C.A.L.L. has also reflected Altadena’s rich African American and Latino history, with generations of players, families and coaches sharing the fields and sustaining youth baseball in the community. The Dreamfields connect that history to another generation of children — perhaps another Jackie Robinson among them — who need places to play, gather and simply be children. C.A.L.L. President Phillip Pollerana said Altadena is excited to get Farnsworth operating again. For Little League families — and a community filled with Dodgers fans — the Dodgers organization’s investment carries practical and symbolic meaning. Dart Cathirell, founder of the Altadena Baseball Academy, is especially pleased the project will include new scoreboards and shaded stands. Cathirell and his coaches have spent years providing young players with instruction, mentorship and opportunities to develop their skills and love of baseball. Those details — scoreboards, shade, fencing and quality playing surfaces — might seem small compared with the enormous challenge of rebuilding Altadena. They are not. Recovery is not simply the reconstruction of houses. Parks, schools, churches, libraries, ballfields and local businesses are connective tissue. They transform a collection of houses into a community. Restoring them gives displaced families another reason to return and gives children back places that defined their lives before the fire. We have already seen that power at Loma Alta Park. Its two Dodgers Dreamfields gave C.A.L.L. a place to play while Farnsworth remained unusable. The 2025 season became extraordinary: Central Altadena’s Braves won the District 17 Tournament of Champions, the first division championship in league history. Altadena’s recovery cannot be measured only by building permits or reconstructed houses. It must also be measured by whether families return, longtime institutions survive, children have safe places to play and neighbors again have places to engage one another.The Dodgers Foundation’s investment cannot solve all of Altadena’s rebuilding challenges. But it demonstrates what meaningful partnership can look like: listening to residents, investing substantial resources and building something intended to endure after the immediate disaster response has faded. Children will run onto the fields at Farnsworth again. Parents will settle into shaded stands. Baseballs will hit gloves, runs will illuminate new scoreboards, and coaches will teach another generation the game. Beyond the ballfields, families will return to Farnsworth’s playgrounds and courts and community life will return to the Davies Building and amphitheater. Against the San Gabriel Mountains, Farnsworth can once again become a place where Altadena gathers. For a community rebuilding from unimaginable loss, we should expect that future, invest in it and work together to make it happen. It will mean a piece of Altadena has returned home.
